## Why Python for Genomics Visualization? {.smaller .scrollable}

[The Python viz stack]{.eyebrow}

### One language, full pipeline

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Python's strengths in bioinformatics:**

::: fragment
**Ecosystem breadth**

- One language for the full pipeline: parsing → analysis → visualization
- Direct integration with `scikit-learn`, `scanpy`, `biopython`
- Reproducible notebooks with Jupyter / Quarto
:::

::: fragment
**Interactivity out of the box**

- Plotly, Bokeh, Panel for web-ready figures
- DashBio for genomics-specific widgets
:::

::: fragment
**Publication quality**

- Matplotlib + Seaborn: journal-grade static figures
- Fine-grained control over every visual element
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: fragment
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# The whole pipeline in one language
import pandas as pd            # data wrangling
import numpy as np             # numerics
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # static plots
import seaborn as sns          # statistical plots
import plotly.express as px    # interactive plots

# Genomics-specific
import scanpy as sc            # single-cell
from Bio import SeqIO          # sequence parsing
import pyCirclize              # circos plots
import toytree                 # phylogenetics
```
:::

<!-- slide 36 -->
## From ggplot2 to Python — The Mental Map {.smaller .scrollable}

[From ggplot2 to Python]{.eyebrow}

### Same grammar, different syntax

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**ggplot2 (R)**
Built on the Grammar of Graphics, the same ideas power Python's ecosystem.

| ggplot2 | Python equivalent |
|---------|------------------|
| `aes(color=group)` | color kwarg / palette dict |
| `geom_point()` | `ax.scatter()` |
| `geom_line()` | `ax.plot()` |
| `facet_wrap(~group)` | `fig, axes = plt.subplots()` |
| `theme()` | `rcParams` + `ax.set_*()` |
| `scale_color_manual()` | custom `palette` dict |
| `labs()` | `ax.set_title/xlabel/ylabel()` |
| `ggsave()` | `fig.savefig(..., dpi=300)` |

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: fragment
**The key shift in mindset:**

- ggplot2 maps data aesthetics **declaratively** — you describe *what* to show
- matplotlib/seaborn are **imperative** — you describe *how* to draw it
- seaborn bridges the gap with a high-level API closer to ggplot2
- For exploratory work → seaborn; for full control → matplotlib
:::

::: fragment
> Every ggplot2 figure you've made has a matplotlib equivalent.
> The grammar is the same, only the syntax changes.
:::
:::
::::::

<!-- slide 37 -->
## Same Plot, Three Syntaxes {.smaller}

[From ggplot2 to Python]{.eyebrow}

### First, meet the data

Plotting packages ship example datasets. Load iris straight from seaborn, then peek at it:

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| class-output: df-preview
import seaborn as sns

iris = sns.load_dataset("iris")   # bundled with the package
print(iris.head())                # raw text, not a rendered table
```

::: {.fragment}
Five columns: four measurements plus a `species` label, the column we will map to colour.
:::

<!-- slide 38 -->
## Same Plot, Three Syntaxes {.smaller}

[From ggplot2 to Python]{.eyebrow}

### One scatterplot of iris, three ways

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="33%"}
**matplotlib** · imperative

```{.python code-line-numbers="1,3"}
for sp, g in iris.groupby("species"):
    plt.scatter(g.sepal_length,
                g.sepal_width, label=sp)
plt.legend()
```

You loop the species and add the legend yourself.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**seaborn** · in between

```{.python code-line-numbers="4"}
sns.scatterplot(data=iris,
                x="sepal_length",
                y="sepal_width",
                hue="species")
```

One call. `hue` maps colour for you.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**ggplot2 (R)** · declarative

```{.r code-line-numbers="3"}
ggplot(iris, aes(sepal_length,
                 sepal_width,
                 colour = species)) +
  geom_point()
```

You declare the mapping; R draws it.
:::
::::::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.takeaway}
matplotlib makes you loop and build the legend. seaborn and ggplot2 just declare the colour mapping. Same grammar, different syntax.
:::
:::

<!-- slide 39 -->
## One Plot, Three Libraries {.smaller}

[The Python ecosystem]{.eyebrow}

### Same scatter, three tools, three trade-offs

matplotlib gives control, seaborn gives speed, plotly gives interactivity. Pick by the job, not by habit. Setup once, then plot three ways.

```{python}
#| echo: true
import seaborn as sns

peng = sns.load_dataset("penguins").dropna(
    subset=["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", "species"])
PAL = {"Adelie": BLUE, "Chinstrap": "#C56B4E", "Gentoo": GREEN}
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### matplotlib

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Full control. `plt.subplots()` hands you the figure (the frame) and `ax` (the canvas you draw on); you loop the groups and build the legend yourself.

```{.python code-line-numbers="1|2,9"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for sp, g in peng.groupby("species"):
    ax.scatter(g.bill_length_mm,
               g.bill_depth_mm,
               color=PAL[sp],
               label=sp, s=38)
ax.set_xlabel("bill length (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("bill depth (mm)")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5), facecolor=CREAM)
ax.set_facecolor(CREAM)
for sp, g in peng.groupby("species"):
    ax.scatter(g.bill_length_mm, g.bill_depth_mm,
               color=PAL[sp], label=sp, s=38, alpha=0.85,
               edgecolors="white", linewidths=0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("bill length (mm)"); ax.set_ylabel("bill depth (mm)")
ax.legend(frameon=False, title="species")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

### seaborn

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
One call, statistical defaults baked in. `hue` maps colour for you. Best for fast exploration, and built on matplotlib so you can still tweak afterward.

```{.python code-line-numbers="5"}
sns.scatterplot(
    data=peng,
    x="bill_length_mm",
    y="bill_depth_mm",
    hue="species",
    palette=PAL)
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5), facecolor=CREAM)
ax.set_facecolor(CREAM)
sns.scatterplot(data=peng, x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm",
                hue="species", palette=PAL, s=55, alpha=0.85, ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel("bill length (mm)"); ax.set_ylabel("bill depth (mm)")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```
:::
::::

### plotly

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
Interactive in the browser: hover for values, zoom, pan. `hover_data` adds fields to the tooltip. Best for dashboards and data you explore, not print.

```{.python code-line-numbers="7-8"}
px.scatter(
    peng,
    x="bill_length_mm",
    y="bill_depth_mm",
    color="species",
    color_discrete_map=PAL,
    hover_data=["island",
                "body_mass_g"])
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
fig = px.scatter(peng, x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm",
                 color="species", color_discrete_map=PAL,
                 hover_data=["island", "body_mass_g"],
                 labels={"bill_length_mm": "bill length (mm)",
                         "bill_depth_mm": "bill depth (mm)"})
fig.update_traces(marker=dict(size=8, line=dict(width=0.5, color="white")),
                  opacity=0.85)
fig.update_layout(paper_bgcolor=CREAM, plot_bgcolor=CREAM,
                  font=dict(family="IBM Plex Mono", color=INK, size=12),
                  height=420, margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=10, b=10))
fig.update_xaxes(gridcolor=LINE, zeroline=False)
fig.update_yaxes(gridcolor=LINE, zeroline=False)
fig
```
:::
::::
